paper_metadata.title: An introduction to financial option pricing on a qudit-based quantum computer

summary: The paper presents a simulated qudit-based implementation of the quantum amplitude-estimation algorithm for European call option pricing under the Black–Scholes–Merton model. Using maximum-likelihood amplitude estimation with T = 7 levels and N = 100 shots per circuit (≈26,200 oracle calls), the simulation shows that the estimated payoff converges to classical discretized results for modest qudit Hilbert-space dimensions (e.g., d = 8–10), while theoretically retaining the O(M^-1) convergence advantage over classical Monte Carlo O(M^-1/2).

experiments.description: Numerical simulation of a qudit-based European call option pricing algorithm using probability loading, comparator, payoff encoding, and amplitude estimation without phase estimation (maximum-likelihood estimation), evaluated for different qudit register dimensions and two parameter settings of the Black-Scholes-Merton model.

algorithm.variant: Amplitude estimation without phase estimation for qudit-based option pricing

hyperparameters.alpha: 0.07 (Fig. 6), 0.07 (Fig. 7 implied same as Fig. 6 unless otherwise stated)
hyperparameters.register_dimension: d varied (examples shown: 8-dimensional and 10-dimensional asset-price registers)

algorithm.parameter_initialization: Not reported; state preparation uses Householder transformation for probability loading

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Asset prices discretized onto a d^n-dimensional qudit register; each basis state |i> encodes a sampled asset price s_i. Comparator ancilla encodes whether i >= k, and payoff qubit encodes the call payoff via controlled Y rotations.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate discounted expected payoff nu = e^{-rT} E_P[max(0, S_T - K)] via amplitude estimation; recover E_P[f(S_T)] from measured payoff-qubit probability P1.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Truncation of the asset-price domain to [Smin, Smax]; payoff scaling and shifting to fit rotation-angle constraints; comparator-based conditional encoding of max(0, S_T-K).

problem_instance.description: European call option pricing under the Black-Scholes-Merton model for a single asset, with simulations shown for two parameter sets and varying qudit register dimension.

dataset_specification.description: Log-normal asset-price distribution sampled at discrete points; no real market dataset used.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Truncate asset-price domain to [Smin, Smax] using 3-sigma rule; discretize into dn equal intervals; sample at interval midpoints; normalize sampled probabilities.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Numerical simulation of the full stack; compare quantum-simulated expected payoff against analytic payoff and finite-resource classical discretization; figures show results versus total Hilbert space dimension.

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Classical sampling of the BSM distribution, truncation, discretization, normalization, and construction of Householder state-preparation matrix.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Maximum-likelihood estimation of theta_P1 from measurement counts; map theta_P1 to P1 and then to expected payoff and option value.

speedup_claims.conditions: amplitude estimation without phase estimation; asymptotic regime
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper states the error scales as O(M^-1) versus O(M^-1/2) classically, but does not provide a numerical empirical speedup factor.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(M^-1) estimation error with M oracle calls; quadratic speedup over classical Monte Carlo

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not quantified; depends on number of oracle calls M where amplitude estimation O(M^-1) beats classical Monte Carlo O(M^-1/2).
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Requires fault‑tolerant implementation of amplitude estimation with repeated Grover operator applications and efficient state preparation for the asset distribution; simulation example used M = 26,200 oracle calls (T = 7, N = 100).
limiting_factors: State preparation of arbitrary probability distributions can scale exponentially with register size
Amplitude estimation requires many coherent oracle calls
Comparator and payoff circuits add additional depth and ancillas
No hardware demonstration; results are purely numerical simulations
Quadratic speedup only (insufficient under Hoefler constant‑factor analysis with error‑correction overhead)

notes: Hardware inferred as simulator_other because the paper states the entire stack is numerically simulated with a custom Python package and does not name a physical QPU.
num_qubits not explicitly given as a single total; the paper describes n qudits plus comparator/payoff ancillas, but does not provide a concrete total qubit count for the simulations.
Circuit depth not reported numerically; only qualitative resource comments and asymptotic scaling are given.
Paper explicitly states the algorithm provides a quadratic speedup over classical Monte Carlo (Sections 2 and 2.3).
All results are numerical simulations using a custom Python package (Section 3), not hardware experiments.
